name: The Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy
statement: Fire wildly, then draw the bullseye around the tightest cluster and call yourself a marksman.
statementAccent: draw the bullseye around the tightest cluster
meaning: The Texas sharpshooter fallacy is a fallacy of inferring meaning from what is essentially a random distribution of data. It is committed when someone finds a pattern or cluster in noisy data after the fact and presents it as if it were meaningful or predicted in advance, cherry-picking the frame afterward while ignoring the data that does not fit. The name comes from a joke about a Texan who fires many shots at the side of a barn, then paints a target centered on the tightest cluster of bullet holes, making himself look like a crack marksman. Related to the clustering illusion, apophenia, and the multiple-comparisons problem in statistics, it exploits the fact that in enough random data some coincidental cluster is bound to appear, then treats that coincidence as significant.
mechanism: The fallacy reverses the proper order of hypothesis and evidence. Instead of specifying a hypothesis in advance and testing it, the arguer looks at where the data happened to land, draws the target around a cluster, and declares a hit. In any large body of random data, some clusters and coincidences will occur by chance, so finding one proves nothing unless the frame was fixed beforehand. Statistically this is the multiple-comparisons problem, or data dredging and p-hacking: test enough hypotheses and some will appear significant by luck alone. It draws on the clustering illusion, the human tendency to see patterns in randomness, and apophenia. A classic case is treating a local disease cluster near a facility as caused by it, when such clusters arise by chance across many places tested.

examples.text: A shooter fires many rounds at a barn, then paints a target around the densest cluster of holes, manufacturing the appearance of accuracy after the fact.
Reading a local cluster of an illness as caused by a nearby facility can be this fallacy, since such clusters occur by chance when many places and conditions are examined.
Testing hundreds of conditions and reporting the one that reaches significance, ignoring the rest, is the statistical face of the fallacy, a multiple-comparisons artifact.

variants.name: The clustering illusion
variants.text: The cognitive tendency to perceive meaningful patterns in random data, underestimating how often clusters arise by chance, which the fallacy exploits.

variants.name: The multiple-comparisons problem
variants.text: The statistical counterpart, in which testing many hypotheses makes some appear significant by luck, the basis of data dredging and p-hacking.

whyItMatters: The Texas sharpshooter fallacy is important in statistics, epidemiology, and critical thinking about spurious correlations and data dredging, naming a pervasive way that random noise is mistaken for meaningful signal. It underlies flawed claims of disease clusters, dubious subgroup findings in trials, and after-the-fact pattern matching from conspiracy theories to cherry-picked data ranges. Recognising it is central to sound science, motivating practices like pre-registering hypotheses and correcting for multiple comparisons so that a pattern must be specified before, not after, seeing where the data fell.

working.text: specify the hypothesis before looking at where the data landed, since drawing the target around a cluster after the fact proves nothing.
remember that testing many possibilities makes some cluster appear significant by chance, so correct for multiple comparisons before claiming a real pattern.
treat patterns found by cherry-picking the frame after seeing the data as likely coincidence rather than meaningful signal.

limits: The fallacy is specifically choosing the target or hypothesis after seeing where the data landed, post hoc, while ignoring the data that does not fit; a genuine, pre-specified hypothesis tested against data is not this fallacy, even if it happens to match a cluster, because the frame was fixed in advance. Distinguishing a coincidental cluster from a real effect can require statistical judgement, so labelling a pattern a Texas sharpshooter case is not always clear-cut. Its precise coinage is uncertain, with the Texas phrasing surfacing in statistical literature around the twentieth century and older shooting analogies from Venn and earlier, so it is a recognised pattern rather than a single-author coinage.
misreadings: The fallacy is choosing the target after seeing the data, cherry-picking a frame in hindsight and ignoring the non-fitting data, not merely finding any pattern. A pre-registered hypothesis tested against data is not this fallacy, even if it matches a cluster, because the prediction came first. And it is not that clusters can never be meaningful; it is that a cluster found by drawing the target around it, in data where clusters arise by chance, is not evidence of a real effect without a frame fixed beforehand.
origin: A statistical and informal fallacy named for the joke of a Texan painting a target around his bullet holes; its precise coinage is unclear, with the Texas phrasing appearing in twentieth-century statistical literature and older shooting analogies from John Venn and earlier.
